questions.q: In the seventeenth century there were two competing theories of light. What could Christiaan Huygens's wave theory explain that Isaac Newton's particle (corpuscular) theory could not?
options: Reflection and refraction of light
Diffraction and interference of light
The speed of light travelling through a vacuum
The straight-line propagation of a light ray
questions.explanation: Newton said light consisted of small particles he called 'corpuscles', and his theory could explain reflection and refraction. Huygens argued light consisted of waves, which was able to explain diffraction and interference — something Newton's particle theory could not do. That is why diffraction and interference remain strong evidence in favour of the wave model.

questions.q: When light bends towards the normal as it enters water (a denser medium), how do Newton's particle model and Huygens's wave model differ in their explanation of the speed of light in water?
options: Both models predict that light travels faster in water than in air
The particle model says light travels faster in water, whereas the wave model says it travels slower
The particle model says light travels slower in water, whereas the wave model says it travels faster
Both models predict that light travels at the same speed in water as in air
questions.explanation: There is a clear distinction between the two models of refraction: the particle model says light bends towards the normal because it travels faster in the denser medium, whereas the wave model says it is because the light is travelling slower. This opposite, testable prediction about the speed of light in water is what makes refraction able to decide between the models.

questions.q: Who measured the speed of light in water in 1850, and what did the result show about Newton's particle model and Huygens's wave model?
options: Newton; light was faster in water, confirming the particle model
Foucault and Fizeau; light was slower in water, confirming the wave model
Thomas Young; light was faster in water, confirming the particle model
Heinrich Hertz; the speed was the same, confirming neither model
questions.explanation: Jean Bernard Leon Foucault and Hippolyte Fizeau competed to measure the speed of light in water; in 1850 both showed that light was slower in water, though Foucault won by seven weeks. Light being slower in water refutes Newton's particle model and confirms Huygens's wave model of refraction.

questions.q: Observations of the polarisation of light show that light is a transverse wave rather than a longitudinal wave. Why does polarisation establish this?
options: Because transverse waves travel faster than longitudinal waves through a polarising filter
Because longitudinal waves cannot be polarised — only a transverse wave has a plane of oscillation that a filter can select
Because a polarising filter slows longitudinal waves down until they stop
Because light, unlike other waves, has no plane of oscillation to filter
questions.explanation: Polarisation is the blocking of waves except for a single plane of oscillation, and it only works with transverse waves. A longitudinal wave oscillates along its direction of travel, so it cannot be polarised. Because light can be polarised, it must be a transverse wave — a result that corrected Huygens, who had proposed that light was longitudinal like sound.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser, then through an analyser whose axis is at 60° to the polariser. Using Malus's law, find the intensity of the emerging polarised light as a percentage of I₀.
questions.given: Unpolarised light intensity \(I_0\); analyser axis at 60° to the polariser; Malus's law \(I = I_O\cos^2\theta\)
working: First filter (light still unpolarised): the polariser halves the intensity, so \(I_a = 0.5\,I_0\)
Second filter (now use Malus's law): \(I_b = I_a\cos^2(60^\circ)\)
questions.explanation: This follows the textbook Sample Problem exactly: a polariser receiving unpolarised light always transmits half (50%), then Malus's law multiplies the emerging polarised intensity by \(\cos^2(60^\circ) = 0.25\), giving 12.5% of the original intensity I₀.

questions.q: A polariser and an analyser are crossed at 90° to each other. Using Malus's law, what intensity of polarised light emerges from the analyser, expressed as a percentage of the polarised intensity falling on it?
questions.given: Crossed polarising filters: angle between axes \(\theta = 90^\circ\); Malus's law \(I = I_O\cos^2\theta\)
questions.explanation: When the polariser and the analyser are crossed at 90°, none of the polarised light is able to pass through the analyser: \(I_d = I_O\cos^2(90^\circ) = 0\). This total extinction of light by crossed polarising filters is itself evidence that light is a transverse wave.

questions.q: From memory: in terms of crests and troughs, distinguish between constructive interference and destructive interference of two identical waves, and say why the dark bands matter.
keyPoints: Constructive interference: two crests (or two troughs) intersect and add, producing an extra-high crest or extra-low trough — greater displacement.
Destructive interference: a crest from one wave meets the trough of another identical wave, giving no wave displacement at all.
If interference occurs with light it produces bands of light and dark; the dark bands prove light is a wave, because two streams of particles can only add, never cancel.
questions.explanation: Diffraction rarely occurs without some interference. Where a crest meets a crest the waves reinforce (constructive); where a crest meets a trough they cancel to zero displacement (destructive). The production of dark bands — darkness from two beams of light — is the decisive evidence that light consists of waves.

questions.q: From memory: recall the DIP memory hook for the three pieces of evidence for the wave model, and for each one give the single reason the particle model fails.
keyPoints: Diffraction: particles travel in straight lines and have no mechanism to bend around a corner into a shadow.
Interference: particles can only add to give brightness, never cancel to give the dark bands.
Polarisation: a particle stream has no plane of oscillation to filter, and only a transverse wave can be polarised.
questions.explanation: DIP — picture the wave model taking a dip — fixes the three pillars so you can't blank on one under exam pressure. Each pillar is written as observation plus why the particle model cannot answer it.

questions.q: The NESA verb 'evaluate' requires more than listing diffraction, interference and polarisation. State the two things an evaluation must include that a bare list does not, and give the wave model's limitation. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: To evaluate, you must first state a clear verdict — a judgement of how strongly the evidence supports the wave model: it is strongly supported for classical light behaviour. Second, you must give the model's limitation. The wave model fails to explain black-body radiation (the classical theory predicts the ultraviolet catastrophe) and the photoelectric effect, both of which require light to behave as discrete particles, photons, in the quantum model. Therefore the wave model is strongly supported but not a complete description of light.

criteria.descriptor: States that an evaluation must give a clear verdict/judgement on how strongly the evidence supports the wave model.
Identifies the limitation: the wave model fails to explain black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect.
Concludes the model is strongly supported for classical light but is not a complete description (light also behaves as photons).

questions.explanation: A list of phenomena scores low; the marks for 'evaluate' come from the verdict plus the limitation. Naming black-body radiation and the photoelectric effect as the failures that need the photon is what turns a list into an evaluation.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, the light reaching the two pinholes had to be coherent. What does coherent mean?
options: The two beams have exactly the same brightness
The light is monochromatic (a single wavelength) and in a fixed phase relationship
The two beams travel in exactly the same direction
The light is polarised in the same plane at both slits
questions.explanation: Young deliberately used a single source (the hole in the blind) so that one wavefront arrived at both pinholes, making the two sources coherent — meaning monochromatic and in phase. Two separate sources would have been incoherent, with a random phase relationship and no discernible interference pattern on the screen.
